rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while limiting run time. The high final organic fraction reduces the risk of unobserved late compounds.

Test temperature-driven selectivity at the same gradient, targeting the crowded central cluster and nearly coeluting final pair. The short initial elution window leaves room to use a shallower gradient later.

Use a shallower gradient at the better-performing temperature to spread the central cluster and test slope-dependent selectivity. The current last peak at 4.71 minutes provides substantial room before the time penalty begins.

The shallower gradient resolved the central cluster but left one near-coelution. Lower temperature by one step to shift that pair's selectivity while aiming to retain the other six resolved gaps and keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test an intermediate slope at 60 C to move the late near-coelution away from its 24-minute-gradient crossing. This may preserve sufficient central-cluster resolution while keeping all peaks comfortably below 10 minutes.

Slightly steepen the gradient relative to injection 5 to improve the remaining critical pair while preserving the central separations. The observed slope response suggests this setting could bring all pairs close to or above R = 1.5.

This increases the slope slightly from 0.04444 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute, targeting the remaining R = 1.49 pair while retaining the central separations. All peaks should elute during the gradient, before the lower final organic fraction becomes limiting.

Injection 7 reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction one step while preserving gradient slope to test whether full resolution can be retained with earlier elution.

Make the gradient one step longer to recover the central separations lost at the higher starting organic fraction. This tests a potentially faster fully resolved alternative while retaining injection 7 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction improves central-cluster selectivity enough to permit a steeper gradient and earlier final elution. Injection 7 remains the fully resolved, maximum-CRF benchmark.

Increase the slope slightly from the fully resolved injection 7, from 0.045 to 0.04583 organic fraction per minute, to test the shortest-elution boundary. The central pairs may approach R = 1.5; injection 7 remains the fallback if resolution drops below target.

The faster-slope boundary at 60 C has been reached, so retain injection 7 as the maximum-score method. Scout 25 C to test whether a different selectivity pattern could enable a shorter fully resolved separation.

The 25 C scout gave promising selectivity with only two unresolved pairs. Lengthen the gradient to test whether both can reach R = 1.5 while keeping the final peak near or below the 7.45-minute benchmark.

At 25 C, simply slowing the gradient worsened the central near-coelution. Test a higher starting organic fraction to change selectivity and shorten retention, retaining injection 7 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Continue the promising higher-starting-organic direction at 25 C. The shallower slope may improve the late critical pair while the increased starting fraction may preserve central selectivity and shorten elution further.
Lengthen the gradient one step to improve the late R = 1.49 pair and test whether the central R = 1.23 gap opens as well. This could yield full resolution substantially earlier than injection 7.
Injection 16 achieved full resolution with the last peak at 4.14 minutes. Raise temperature one step to test a faster separation while monitoring the two smallest resolution margins.

Return to 25 C and test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient. This may shorten final elution while compensating for the central resolution loss seen when increasing starting organic alone.
Halve the slope at the higher starting organic fraction to test whether the remaining central pair can reach R = 1.5. Injection 16 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Refine between injections 15 and 16 with a slope of 0.055 organic fraction per minute. This tests whether full resolution can be retained with a last peak earlier than 4.14 minutes; injection 16 remains the fallback.

Test an intermediate starting organic fraction to balance the two central gaps, using a slope expected to keep the late pair near baseline resolution. This explores a potentially faster fully resolved alternative while preserving injection 16 as the current fastest maximum-score method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 21 to shorten elution and improve the marginal late pair. The central selectivity differs from the 0.35 starting-fraction method, so this tests whether its larger central gap can tolerate the temperature increase.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction moves the central pair beyond its selectivity crossing and enables a shorter resolved separation. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Refine around the fastest fully resolved method, injection 16, with a slightly shallower gradient to increase resolution margins. This targets a more robust maximum-score alternative while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Use the final injection to test a compromise between the fastest fully resolved method, injection 16, and the larger resolution margins of injection 24. This intermediate slope should retain the maximum CRF with earlier elution than injection 24.
